summary: This document describes methods for handling Unicode strings that represent usernames and passwords. It replaces the older SASLprep approach from RFC 4013, which was based on Stringprep in RFC 3454, with a more sustainable approach based on PRECIS.

plainLanguage.summary: User names and passwords can contain any character from any writing system, and handling them carelessly creates security holes. This document defines three sets of rules: one for user names that ignores letter case, one for user names that keeps it, and one for passwords that keeps every character as the user typed it. A protocol adopts one of these sets and applies the same steps everywhere, so that the same name is always recognised as the same name.

questions: how to handle unicode in passwords
why normalize a username with nfc
subtitle: How to handle usernames and passwords that contain letters and symbols from every script.

tldr.problem: Usernames and passwords are Unicode strings, and naive handling of them lets two different strings look and compare as the same, which makes account spoofing possible.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two PRECIS profiles for usernames, one that folds case and one that keeps it, plus an OpaqueString profile for passwords, each with fixed preparation, enforcement and comparison rules.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 7613 and the older SASLprep profile it built on. It is meant for application protocols to adopt one profile at a time, and it warns that mixed deployments hurt interoperability.

today: RFC 8265 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current PRECIS-based treatment of internationalized usernames and passwords. It replaced RFC 7613, which in turn had replaced the SASLprep profile of Stringprep defined in RFC 4013.

sections.title: Why These Rules Exist
sections.content:
Usernames and passwords are widely used for authentication and authorization on the Internet, either directly when provided in plaintext, as in the PLAIN SASL mechanism and the HTTP Basic scheme, or indirectly when provided as the input to a cryptographic algorithm such as a hash function, as in the SCRAM SASL mechanism and the HTTP Digest scheme.

To increase the likelihood that the input and comparison of usernames and passwords work in ways that make sense for typical users throughout the world, the document defines rules for handling internationalized strings. Such strings consist of code points from the Unicode coded character set, with special attention to code points outside the ASCII range. The rules are specified through profiles of the string classes defined in the PRECIS framework, RFC 8264.

These profiles are designed in large measure to protect application developers from the negative consequences of supporting the full range of Unicode code points. In almost all application protocols it would be dangerous to treat the code point for SUPERSCRIPT ONE, U+00B9, as equivalent to DIGIT ONE, U+0031, because that would result in false accepts during comparison, authentication and authorization. An attacker could then easily spoof an account. Similar considerations apply to passwords, although there it is desirable to support a wider range of characters so as to maximize entropy for authentication.

The historical predecessor of the document was the SASLprep profile of Stringprep, but the approach defined here can be used by technologies other than SASL, such as HTTP authentication. The document does not modify the handling of internationalized strings in existing application protocols that use SASLprep; a community that wants to modernize must explicitly update the protocol definition, and non-coordinated updates are discouraged because they can hurt interoperability and security.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters look like ordinary letters but are not the same character, so a program that compares them loosely can be tricked into accepting the wrong account. These rules pick a safe subset of characters and define exactly how to convert them before comparing, so that every implementation ends up with the same result.

sections.title: Usernames, Passwords and Userparts
sections.content:
A username, or user identifier, is a string of characters designating an account on a computing device or system, often but not necessarily for use by a person. Some devices allow a username to be part or all of a person's name, but because of the complexities involved, that outcome is not guaranteed for all human names on all systems that follow the rules here. Protocol designers who wish to allow a wider range of characters are encouraged to consider a separation between more restrictive account identifiers and more expressive display names or nicknames.

A password is a string of characters that allows access to a computing device or system, often associated with a particular username. A password is not literally limited to a word, because a password could be a passphrase consisting of more than one word, perhaps separated by spaces, punctuation or other non-alphanumeric characters.

Some SASL mechanisms specify that the authentication identity used in their context is a simple username, and various application technologies assume that the identity of a user or account takes the form of a username, whether or not they use SASL. The exact form of a username in any particular mechanism or application technology is a matter for implementation and deployment, and a username does not necessarily map to any particular application identifier. The term non-ASCII space refers to any Unicode code point with a general category of Zs, naturally with the exception of SPACE, U+0020.
sections.plainLanguage: A username names an account. A password unlocks it. A password may be several words with spaces, so it is not just a single word. The document also separates the account name from any display name, so a name that looks nice on screen does not have to be usable as a login.

sections.title: The Shape of a Username
sections.content:
A username is a string of Unicode code points structured as an ordered sequence of userparts and expressed in a standard Unicode encoding form such as UTF-8. A userpart may contain only code points allowed by the PRECIS IdentifierClass, and thus consists almost exclusively of letters and digits. A username can consist of a single userpart or a space-separated sequence of userparts.

The syntax is username = userpart *(1*SP userpart) and userpart = 1*(idpoint), where an idpoint is a Unicode code point that can be contained in a string conforming to the PRECIS IdentifierClass. All code points and blocks not explicitly allowed in the IdentifierClass are disallowed, including private-use code points, surrogate code points, and the code points and blocks defined as Prohibited Output in RFC 4013. Common constructions such as user@example.com are allowed as usernames, as they were under RFC 4013.

A username MUST NOT be zero bytes in length, and this rule is enforced after any normalization and mapping of code points. The document notes that this username construct does not necessarily match what deployed applications call a username or userid, but instead provides a relatively safe subset of Unicode code points that can be used in existing SASL mechanisms and in application protocols that use SASL, and even in most application protocols that do not currently use SASL.
sections.plainLanguage: A username is made of one or more pieces separated by spaces. Each piece may hold only letters, digits and a small set of other characters; everything else, including private-use characters, is refused. The finished username must not be empty.

sections.title: Case Mapping and Case Preservation
sections.content:
The document defines two username profiles that differ only in their use, or lack of use, of the case mapping rule. In UsernameCaseMapped, the width mapping rule maps fullwidth and halfwidth code points to their decomposition mappings, there is no additional mapping rule, the case mapping rule maps uppercase and titlecase code points to their lowercase equivalents, the normalization rule applies Unicode Normalization Form C to all strings, and the directionality rule applies the Bidi Rule to strings that contain right-to-left code points. In UsernameCasePreserved, the width mapping, normalization and directionality rules are the same, but there is no case mapping rule.

Case mapping is a matter for the application protocol, implementation or deployment. In general the document suggests the UsernameCaseMapped profile is preferable, because not doing case mapping can lead to false accepts during authentication and authorization and can result in confusion among end users, given the prevalence of case mapping in many existing protocols. There can be good reasons to use UsernameCasePreserved instead, such as backward compatibility with deployed infrastructure.

Because case mapping results in information loss, implementations SHOULD delay any case mapping to the last possible moment, such as when doing a lookup by username, performing username comparisons, or generating a cryptographic salt from a username. SASL mechanisms are not to apply this or any other profile to authorization identifiers, only to authentication identifiers.

Comparison under both profiles is exact: the two strings are considered equivalent if and only if they are an exact octet-for-octet match, sometimes called bit-string identity. Until an implementation determines whether two strings are to be considered equivalent, it MUST NOT treat them as equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: The two username profiles differ in one thing only. One folds every letter to lower case before comparing, so Alice and alice are the same account. The other leaves the case alone. The document prefers folding, because mixing the two rules between systems leads to accounts that look identical but do not match.

sections.title: The OpaqueString Profile for Passwords
sections.content:
A password is a string of Unicode code points conformant to the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass and expressed in a standard Unicode encoding form. The syntax is password = 1*(freepoint), where a freepoint is a code point that can be contained in a string conforming to the FreeformClass. A password MUST NOT be zero bytes in length, and the rule is enforced after any normalization and mapping. The document notes that this prohibition is not a recommendation about password strength, but is meant to stop applications from omitting a password entirely, since a non-empty sequence of characters can result in a zero-length password after canonicalization.

Preparation ensures the string consists only of code points explicitly allowed in the FreeformClass. Enforcement then applies five rules in order. The width mapping rule states that fullwidth and halfwidth code points MUST NOT be mapped to their decomposition mappings. The additional mapping rule maps any instance of non-ASCII space to SPACE, U+0020, because including only SPACE prevents confusion with the various non-ASCII space code points, many of which are difficult to reproduce across different input methods. The case mapping rule is absent, because mapping uppercase and titlecase code points to lowercase would lead to false accepts and thus reduced security. The normalization rule applies Unicode Normalization Form C to all strings. There is no directionality rule, because the Bidi Rule and similar rules reduce the repertoire of characters that are allowed and therefore the amount of entropy possible in a password.

Comparison under this profile is also exact, an octet-for-octet match. Section 8.2 notes that in systems that conform to modern best practices for security, verification of passwords during authentication will not use this comparison. Because the system performs cryptographic calculations to verify the password, it will prepare and enforce the rules before performing the calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords use a wider set of characters than usernames, so that a longer password can still be random. Every kind of space is turned into a normal space, because the unusual ones are hard to type on another keyboard. Letter case is left exactly as typed, and the final comparison is exact.

sections.title: Where the Rules Are Applied
sections.content:
The document specifies only the PRECIS-based rules for handling strings conforming to the two username profiles and the OpaqueString profile. It is the responsibility of an application protocol to specify the protocol slots in which such strings can appear, the entities expected to enforce the rules, and at what points during protocol processing or interface handling the rules need to be enforced. Application protocols can also define their own rules, such as minimum or maximum length, further restrictions on code points, and safeguards against visually similar characters.

Some PRECIS profile definitions encourage entities that enforce the rules to be liberal in what they accept. For usernames and passwords such a policy can be problematic, because it can lead to false accepts.

Applying the rules for any given PRECIS profile is not necessarily an idempotent procedure for all code points. An implementation SHOULD therefore apply the rules repeatedly until the output string is stable. If the output string does not stabilize after reapplying the rules three additional times after the first application, the implementation SHOULD terminate application of the rules and reject the input string as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol that uses these strings decides which fields they appear in and who checks them. Because some characters change when the rules are applied, a program should keep applying the rules until nothing changes any more, and reject the input if it still keeps changing after a few tries.

sections.title: Migrating from SASLprep
sections.content:
The rules defined in this document differ slightly from those defined by the SASLprep specification, though not from RFC 7613. Deployments that currently use SASLprep for handling usernames might need to scrub existing data when they migrate.

SASLprep specified the use of Unicode Normalization Form KC, whereas the two username profiles employ Unicode Normalization Form C. In practice this change is unlikely to cause significant problems, because the PRECIS IdentifierClass entirely disallows code points with compatibility equivalents, which makes NFC less aggressive about finding matches than NFKC. The RFC gives three examples of compatibility equivalences: LATIN SMALL LETTER LONG S, U+017F, is compatibility equivalent to LATIN SMALL LETTER S, U+0073; ROMAN NUMERAL FOUR, U+2163, is compatibility equivalent to LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I, U+0049 and LATIN CAPITAL LETTER V, U+0056; and LATIN SMALL LIGATURE FI, U+FB01, is compatibility equivalent to LATIN SMALL LETTER F, U+0066 and LATIN SMALL LETTER I, U+0069. Operators might search their database for such code points and map them where there is no conflict, but they may find conflicting usernames, for instance HENRYIV against HENRYⅣ, and then need to decide how to proceed, for example by disabling the account whose name contains a code point with a compatibility equivalent.

SASLprep also mapped the characters commonly mapped to nothing to nothing, whereas the IdentifierClass disallows most of them. For migration purposes, the operator might want to remove those code points, such as SOFT HYPHEN, U+00AD, from usernames, because in practice a user would not notice the difference if they were removed. Finally, SASLprep allowed uppercase and titlecase code points, whereas the UsernameCaseMapped profile maps them to lowercase, while the UsernameCasePreserved profile matches SASLprep in this regard.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules folded some characters together that the new rules keep apart, so a migration can turn two existing accounts into one. The document tells operators to look for those characters in their database and decide case by case what to do before switching over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ability to include a wide range of characters in passwords and passphrases can increase the potential for creating a strong password with high entropy. In practice, the ability to include such characters ought to be weighed against the possible need to reproduce them on various devices using various input methods.

Comparing identifiers, such as SASL simple usernames, authentication identifiers and authorization identifiers, can lead to either false rejects or false accepts, both of which have security implications. A false reject means a legitimate user is refused; a false accept means a wrong name is let in, and an account such as user1@example.com could be spoofed by a name that only looks the same.

The security considerations described in RFC 8264 apply to the IdentifierClass and FreeformClass string classes used in this document, and the security considerations described in Unicode Technical Standard #39 apply to the use of Unicode code points in usernames and passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: The security risk is in the comparison, not in the characters themselves. A rule that is too loose lets two different names match, and a rule that is too tight locks a real user out. The document points to the PRECIS framework and the Unicode security standard for the detailed analysis.
